prompt.context: Our client is a multi-billion dollar liquor distributor. It has hired a consultant to determine why its whisky brand is not growing.
prompt.question: Why is the client's whisky brand not growing, and what should the client do about it?

clarifying_info.q: How is the whisky market segmented?
clarifying_info.a: There is a high, medium, and low end of the market. The high end has 10 competitors (5 new), the medium end has 2 including the client, and the low end has 4 competitors.

clarifying_info.q: How is each market segment growing?
clarifying_info.a: The high end is growing at 14%, the low end is growing at 8%, and the medium range is contracting at 6%.

clarifying_info.q: Has market share changed or have new products been introduced in the medium segment?

clarifying_info.a: The client has two types of drinkers: 70% are males aged 40-55 who like taste and brand, enjoy a drink after work, and drink whisky straight or on the rocks. 30% are younger males and females aged 21-35 who are part of the bar and club crowd and drink whisky mixed.

clarifying_info.q: Has the client changed its product, price, or marketing recently?
clarifying_info.a: Marketing has been consistent. Distillers recently changed ingredients to save $0.25 per bottle on COGS but have not changed the taste. The client also recently raised price from $11 to $12.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competition priced at in the medium range?
clarifying_info.a: Competitors in the medium range are priced at $11.

framework: External analysis: Competition — market share changes, new entrants, segmentation, market growth by segment
External analysis: Customers — who are they, what do they want, are preferences shifting
Internal analysis: Product — any changes to product, ingredients, or formulation
Internal analysis: Pricing — price changes vs. competitors
Internal analysis: Marketing — any changes to brand messaging or spend

questions.prompt: What does the competitive and market data tell you about the client's situation?
questions.guidance: The client is in the medium segment, which is the only segment contracting (-6%). High end (+14%) and low end (+8%) are both growing. No share shifts or new products in the medium segment, so the contraction is structural. The client needs to consider moving out of the medium segment.

questions.prompt: What do the customer segmentation data tell you, and what implications does the price increase have for each customer group?
questions.guidance: 70% of customers are older males (40-55) who value taste, brand, and tradition — they have high brand loyalty and could migrate to the high end. 30% are younger bar-crowd customers (21-35) who drink whisky mixed and are likely price-sensitive with low brand loyalty. Raising price from $11 to $12 (a ~9% increase) while the only medium competitor stays at $11 would disproportionately drive away the price-sensitive bar crowd. The loyalty of the older segment may allow them to follow the brand upmarket.

math.setup: Price increase: $12 - $11 = $1 per bottle; percentage increase = $1 / $11 ≈ 9.1%
math.answer: ~9% price premium over the only medium competitor

questions.prompt: What did the ingredient change save, and does it justify the price increase?
questions.guidance: COGS savings of $0.25 per bottle. The client simultaneously raised price by $1, so the net margin improvement per bottle is $1.00 (price increase) + $0.25 (COGS reduction) = $1.25 per bottle, assuming volume holds. However, if the price increase is driving volume loss, the overall revenue and profit impact could be negative.

math.setup: Per-bottle economics of the two changes
math.answer: $1.25/bottle improvement per unit sold, but volume loss likely offsets this

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic options should the client consider to return to growth?

categories.name: Enter high end
ideas: Launch a premium line targeting the 70% loyal male segment aged 40-55
Reposition the existing brand with upgraded packaging and premium pricing
Acquire or partner with an existing premium whisky brand
Invest in heritage and craftsmanship storytelling to justify premium price

categories.name: Enter low end
ideas: Introduce a value brand extension for the 21-35 bar and club crowd
Price a sub-brand below $11 to compete directly with low-end players
Market as a mixer-friendly whisky to capture the mixed-drink occasion

categories.name: Defend the medium segment
ideas: Revert price to $11 to match the remaining medium competitor
Differentiate on product attributes to justify the $1 premium
Increase marketing spend to reinforce brand loyalty in the medium segment

categories.name: Pricing and COGS
ideas: Reverse the price increase to $11 while retaining the $0.25 COGS saving
Use the COGS saving to fund marketing rather than pass it to margin

recommendation: The client should exit the contracting medium segment and pursue a two-pronged strategy: (1) launch or reposition a premium brand targeting the loyal 70% male segment aged 40-55, who have strong brand affinity and are gravitating toward the high end; (2) consider a value brand extension to capture the 30% bar-crowd segment that is migrating to the low end due to price sensitivity.

In the short term, the client should reverse its price increase back to $11 (or justify the $12 price through clear premium positioning) to stem immediate volume loss to the only remaining medium competitor.
risks: Brand dilution if the client operates across multiple price tiers simultaneously
Execution risk in premiumization — the high end has 10 competitors including 5 new entrants
The low-end extension may cannibalize the existing medium brand
Reverting price may signal weakness and reduce margin
next_steps: Conduct customer research to confirm willingness-to-pay and brand perception among the 70% loyal segment
Model volume and margin scenarios for a premium launch vs. a low-end extension vs. defending the medium
Benchmark high-end competitor positioning to identify whitespace for premiumization
